findings.title: The design drops the structured-output requirement that the plan and architecture assign to this slice
findings.description:
The slice plan's success criteria for 302 include: "The score-with-rationale shape is enforced by the template's structured output." The architecture also commits to this (Technical Considerations, reliability item (b)): "the judge template uses a structured-output constraint for the score field and a score-with-rationale prompt shape."

The design only gives prompt instructions plus the lenient `score:` parser. It also says `## Rationale` "is prose scaffolding for the model, not a new parser target" (lines 180-183). So nothing enforces the rationale, and nothing constrains the score field. A response with a bare `score:` and no justification passes. This is one of the architecture's few in-engine mitigations against anchoring, so it can't be quietly dropped.

Either:
- name the structured-output mechanism the template uses (for example, an output-schema or response-format field on the template, if the review engine supports one), or
- say explicitly that this slice defers the criterion, give the reason, and record it in the slice plan's Future Work so the gap is tracked.

findings.title: The `sq review` CLI path that the design relies on doesn't exist, and the design rules out changing the CLI
findings.description:
The Value section (lines 31-33), Functional Requirement 3 (lines 277-282) and walkthrough step 3 (lines 361-379) all assume a CLI form like `sq review slice-vs-arch … --template judge.slice-vs-arch`. The current `sq review` subcommands are `slice`, `arch`, `tasks`, `code` and `list`. Each one hard-codes its template name, and none takes a `--template` option. The design's note that the CLI shape "should be confirmed during implementation" (lines 376-379) hides a real gap.

That conflicts with "What changes" (lines 39-57) and "No other module changes" (line 107). As written, Functional Requirement 3 can't be met. Pick one:
- **(a)** Run the requirement and walkthrough through a pipeline `review` step, the selection path the architecture actually commits to, and remove the CLI claims from Value and Functional Requirement 3.
- **(b)** Add a minimal `--template` option to the relevant review commands as an explicit, listed change.

Option (a) is lighter and matches the architecture.

findings.title: The failure-mode table leaves out two failure modes the architecture lists
findings.description:
The architecture lists these judge failure modes: unparseable response; score absent or outside 0–100; **missing/unreadable ground-truth file**; provider unavailable; **injected ground truth exceeding the cap**. The slice's table claims to give "the mapping … explicit for these specific paths," but it has no row for either of the two in bold.

The `TEMPLATE_INPUTS` row only covers a `SliceInfo` with a missing field. It doesn't cover a path that resolves but points to a file that doesn't exist. That case matters here because the new `judge.tasks-vs-slice` entry reuses `_tasks_input`, which builds the path from `task_files[0]` without checking that the file exists. Each of these rows can simply say "inherited from the review path → `UNKNOWN`, WARNING log." But the no-silent-pass guarantee is only stated, not shown, until those rows are there. Add both rows and name the existing handler for each.

findings.title: The data-flow example uses the wrong pass floor for `judge.slice-vs-arch`
findings.description: The example shows `score=82 ≥ pass_floor(78)` for `judge.slice-vs-arch`. The thresholds table (lines 223-226) and the walkthrough give that template `pass_floor` 82. 78 belongs to `judge.tasks-vs-slice`. The outcome is still PASS, but fix the number so tests aren't copied from the wrong value.

findings.title: The "rogue verdict is discarded" test re-tests slice 301
findings.description: `enforce_judge` never reads `result.verdict`. That is slice 301's contract, and 301's tests already cover it. Re-testing it here with a hand-built `ReviewResult` doesn't exercise anything this slice adds. Whether the model actually leaves out the verdict can only be seen in a live run, and the Mitigation section already plans for that. Drop this test, or replace it with a check that each template's system prompt contains the no-verdict instruction.
